data.title: The tragedy of a successful conquest of the homeland – a Hungarian view
data.excerpt: Thanks to our collaborator Mrs Kveta M. we bring you a translation of a very interesting article from the Hungarian site archeologia.hu. It is one of the few texts that are beginning to chip away at the Hungarian myth of a heroic conquest of an almost empty Carpathian Basin, and it confronts the archaeologically attested presence of the Slavs and the continuity of their occupation after the arrival of the Hungarians.
data.metaTitle: The tragedy of a successful conquest of the homeland
data.metaDescription: A translated Hungarian article that questions the myth of an empty Carpathian Basin and of the heroic conquest of the homeland by the Magyars.

children.text: Thanks to our collaborator Mrs Kveta M. we bring you a translation of a very interesting article published on the Hungarian site
http://archeologia.hu/egy-sikeres-honfoglalas-tragediaja

It can be counted among the small number of articles that have lately been appearing, hesitantly, among our southern neighbours and that are slowly beginning to chip away at the entrenched Hungarian myths about the heroic conquest of the homeland and the periods that followed. The article makes it clear that today's Hungarians (at least part of the scholarly community) have to come to terms with the undoubted, archaeologically attested presence of the Slavs in the Carpathian Basin in the Early Middle Ages and with the continuity of their occupation even after the arrival of the Hungarians. You can also read about the Slavic occupation of Visegrád in this separate article:
Visegrád.

In the Solomon Tower at Visegrád an exhibition is opening about the almost unknown past of Hungary, about the earlier wanderings of the Hungarians before the conquest of the homeland and about their adaptation to life among the peoples of the Carpathian Basin. In our own interest we must rid ourselves of many centuries-old false illusions.

The forthcoming exhibition has been prepared in cooperation between the Hungarian Academy of Sciences and the King Matthias Museum at Visegrád. The exhibition will show the results of research which in recent years has „redrawn“ the scholarly view of the history of the Hungarians before the conquest of the homeland and aroused a great response in the press, and also the results of new research which here at Visegrád can illustrate historical events from Carolingian times to the foundation of the state. On the basis of this research there emerges a hitherto largely unknown picture of the 8th–10th centuries, which are regarded as a dark (in the sense of: unknown) period of Hungarian history, and this leads us to reformulate everything we have thought for whole centuries about the earliest history of the Hungarian state.

children.text: Look towards the sky!

Isaac Asimov – one of the best science-fiction writers… wrote, among other things, an essay on the tragedy of the Moon… The fact that the Moon rises in the sky and sets from it each day at different places led people to the idea that they stood at the centre of the world (the geocentric world view), and it took a very long time before genuine scientific research arrived at the heliocentric picture of the world, and it even had to fight against dogmatic prevailing opinions…
How does that relate to the conquest of the homeland and to the history of the century before and after it?
The parallel is obvious: one need only look at the noble faces of the conquerors of the homeland on the circular
Feszty panorama painting

, at their dignified bearing… or leaf through a school textbook about the period in question… and it is immediately clear that our ancestors were demigods, that the world revolved around them… and that we, their descendants, cannot be any less perfect either, for after all the same blood flows in us. Just as they had a right to the Carpathian Basin, so we too have a right to the respect of all nations – and if we are not able to achieve that, then let us at least shout at the top of our lungs that it belongs to us.
The conquest of the homeland, or rather its historical assessment, in its fossilised dogmatic loftiness – that is our Moon.

Our historiography is quite cautious when it comes to investigating the whole century before the conquest of the homeland, as well as the decades preceding the foundation of the state. The results of research are in vain when Anonymus's description still holds as the standard, the description of an almost deserted Carpathian Basin which the flood of Hungarians easily appropriated. They meet no resistance, and when they do, they triumph with fairy-tale ease, slaying their enemies.

Magister P. (= Anonymus) could not have hoped that his gesta, which at the time represented belles-lettres rather than anything else, would have such a long-lasting influence. The Germans too at certain times (most recently under the Nazis) regarded their Nibelungs as the source of their historical self-definition – and we know how that ended.

Let us return to the Gesta Hungarorum, which well reflects the historical approach of the aristocracy in the decades around 1200. In the days of Magister P. the royal court was half full of Western Europeans (Frenchmen and Spaniards), who had brought with them their flourishing chivalric culture, romances, troubadour songs and myths of origin reaching back to the times of Charlemagne. It is understandable that the Hungarian aristocracy too longed for a glorious past, for the celebration of heroic deeds of its ancestors, even invented ones. This essentially harmless little vanity, combined with the boundless imagination of Magister P., then filled the Carpathian Basin with invented ancestors and a host of battles that never took place. For history, however, this long represented only a time bomb, for until the middle of the 18th century few people read it. Far greater attention was enjoyed by the gesta of Simon of Kéza, 80 years younger. It sought to create myths of origin for a relatively young (1–2 generations old) noble (gentry) stratum at a time that was not very favourable to them, since they were becoming the victims of the ever stronger upper stratum, the barons. Several authors later continued and supplemented the work of Simon of Kéza, and eventually, in the 14th century, it was also preserved in manuscript form in the (Vienna) Illuminated Chronicle. In the 15th century it also appeared in print and spread in wider circles, so that it was never forgotten. The most influential version of Simon of Kéza's work was the Chronica Hungarorum of John of Thurocz, which also appeared in book form in 2 editions with the support of King Matthias. John of Thurocz had already „reformatted“ the whole conception of the work according to the demands of his own time. A place in it was also given to the history following Simon of Kéza, which created an appearance of credibility for the whole work, at the beginning of which stood the myth of Hunnic beginnings, of the origin of the nation, thoroughly inflated by Simon of Kéza. In this reworking, however, the Hungarians inherited the homeland by right, since it is the same nation. This history begins and ends with great kings (Attila vs. Matthias). The work of John of Thurocz proved a little „coarse“ for the royal court (they therefore had Bonfini draw up his more sophisticated, but no less fanciful version, in which the Avars also appeared), but its influence on society was overwhelming. These are the last decades of the Hungarian Middle Ages, when the lesser and middle nobility strove ever more desperately to defend their privileges, and therefore sought out and guarded their roots. John of Thurocz offered them a splendid defensive shield – practically a millennium of tradition behind their rights, for they could trace their families directly back to the conquerors of the homeland.

children.text: The world of the Hunnic ancestors of the Hungarian nobility might calmly have remained merely an interlude, had the medieval Hungarian state not begun to disintegrate at that time – a state which even at its height lagged behind the Western European states in cultural terms. The Battle of Mohács and the break-up of the country into several parts saw to a long-term freezing of the natural development towards a civic (bourgeois) society, and therefore no demand arose for the creation of a new view of history. During almost 200 years of Turkish rule, and even after the Turks had been driven out of the country, most of the Hungarian nobility was still hibernating in spirit in the period of the early 16th century, failing to understand and rejecting the modernising efforts of the Habsburg monarchy, which manifested themselves in a significant curtailment of noble privileges. Many of these old privileges, regarded as positively ancient, had long since lost their relevance and meaning, but the newly recast spirit of the Hungarian nobility sought to preserve them. Many did not even shrink from allying themselves with the occupying Ottoman Empire on that account. During the 18th century and also in the 19th century, when the hopes resting on the Ottomans had finally evaporated, this lesser-noble outlook and approach to history finally crystallised, until it congealed in public opinion as a dogma, not least because the Habsburg predominance in other fields could be answered in this way alone (by preserving the illusion of ancient greatness). Trianon, the detachment of the historical regions of Hungary, with its undoubted shock effect, again only strengthened the need to cling convulsively to the greatness of times past. Today, however, for a part of the Hungarians not even the heritage of Attila, the Hungarian pyramids in Bosnia and a 30,000-year-old runic script are enough; they need a Parthian-Hungarian Christ. The truth is that a false past will not make the present any better („more liveable“), and the future will be positively hopeless. Yet the reason how and why the Hungarian state was successful from the 9th–10th to the 15th century can easily be uncovered on the basis of our present-day insights as well.
Not a deserted land

Let us return once more to the Carpathian Basin in the 9th century, specifically to Transdanubia, Pannonia, which was an area under Carolingian influence. More recent excavations at already known archaeological sites (Sibrik Hill at Visegrád, the Cella Trichora at Pécs, Zalavár, Fenékpuszta) have all shown the presence of the Carolingian period, traces of building and rebuilding. The anthropological material from 9th-century cemeteries barely differs from that of an 11th-century cemetery. The Hunnic empire was only an interlude in the Carpathian Basin. The Roman authorities and armies did indeed leave the province, and many of those tied to the Roman imperial administration also departed, but the more or less Romanised local population had nowhere to go. On the frontiers opened up by the Huns there appeared newcomers of Germanic and Iranian origin, a considerable part of whom continued westwards, but those who stayed here adapted easily to local conditions, not least because many of them already arrived as Christians. When in the middle of the 6th century the Turkic-speaking Avars from Asia created their multi-ethnic empire covering the whole Carpathian Basin, they had no intention whatsoever of exterminating or driving out the peoples living here; they even endeavoured to have further, if possible trained, craftsmen from the Balkans and Italy settle here. New settlers also came from the north and from the east: Slavs and the Turkic-speaking Onogurs, who in the second half of the 7th century already shaped the character of the whole Avar Empire. This multi-ethnic empire, however, took care that the individual groups of its subjects should not entertain thoughts of possible independence, and therefore it did not look kindly on its subjects living in towns well fortified by the Romans. For a time it did turn a blind eye, especially if the group in question was sufficiently loyal to the empire, as in the case of the Christian community living in prosperity in the fortified town at Fenékpuszta (today we call it the Keszthely culture, made up of mixed Romanised and Germanic elements), but when a conflict arose between this community and the empire, the empire intervened harshly. The Roman fortified town was violently laid waste around the middle of the 7th century, but its inhabitants, now impoverished, could go on living peacefully in its surroundings. Elsewhere too – as we know from the case of ancient Sopianae (Pécs, Pätikostolie in the Late Roman period, translator's note), where the fortified town was of a similar size to that at Fenékpuszta – this town was emptied, but the open (unprotected) settlements of the Romanised population nearby, though outside the fortification, survived for centuries more. At the end of the 8th century, however, the Avar Empire was already losing control of its mounting internal tensions. The Slavs, who had moved in during the preceding century (over the last 100 years), probably behaved just as we know from the better documented Balkan-Byzantine territories: they kept their archaic clan organisation, moved into the more deserted peripheral territories, into wooded hilly areas, and submitted to the Avar Empire only formally, but they readily created their own fortified centres (hillforts), making use of and occupying even such abandoned Roman forts as the stronghold at Visegrád (on Sibrik Hill, translator's note). When the discrepancies in the governance of the empire turned into military conflicts, the force that held together this multilingual, multi-ethnic Avar Empire also passed away, and at the beginning of the 9th century it collapsed completely in practically a few moments. In the anarchic situation that arose, everyone who could took refuge behind the walls of the still well-preserved Roman forts and towns. The population of Transdanubia in all probability gladly welcomed the Carolingians, since they came with the promise of order, peace and security, and also with Christianity, which had not vanished from the territory in question for a single moment during the preceding centuries. Pribina, a prince of Slavic origin in the re-organised province of Pannonia, gathered the local people into the surroundings of Mosaburg; alongside the Slavs these were also the Romanised people of the Keszthely culture, and it is only to chance, and also to Methodius, who was later canonised, that we can owe the fact that the first Pannonian bishopric supervised from Salzburg was not founded at Mosaburg/Zalavár.
The newcomers (new arrivals)

Meanwhile, from the regions of the Southern Urals, a people set out westwards in whose culture the world of the northern Finno-Ugrians was already mingling with the world of the steppes. During the rapid migration (lasting about 1 generation) three tribes from the likewise multi-ethnic Khazar Empire joined them, who were given the name Kabars. In the second half of the 9th century this a priori multicultural society arrived in a country which was by no means deserted, but in which they found a multitude of other peoples and languages: the Turkic-speaking Avars and Bulgars, as well as Slavs belonging to various branches and tribes, Germanic peoples and also descendants of the Roman provincial population. The empire of the late Carolingians was going through a crisis, the Bulgarian empire was fighting for life and death with Byzantium, and so the Carpathian Basin, situated outside the centres of the empires mentioned, became easy prey for the new conquerors. The inhabitants of this multi-ethnic and multilingual land sooner or later adopted the language of the conquerors as well, even though the latter were in fact in a minority. In the new empire founded by the Árpáds it was also necessary to introduce a common mediating language. The ethnogenesis of Hungarian identity did not take place on the steppes, but only in the Carpathian Basin, and its components include equally the Celts, Romans, Germanic peoples, Avars and Slavs who had lived here for centuries, as well as the immigrant Hungarians and Turks (I think that here he means the Kabars and the Proto-Bulgars, translator's note). The fact that from so many different peoples a unified empire could come into being by the end of the 11th century, and that in this empire a unified people took shape by the 12th–13th centuries (translator's note: in the sense of state allegiance it may be so, but certainly not in the sense of a „nation“; that is probably also why the author used the term „people“), happened not least thanks to the fact that part of the Hungarians, the conquerors of the homeland, quickly grasped the situation and the possibilities that this land offered. Taksony, Géza and Stephen achieved success in that they began to lay the foundations of their empire in those Pannonian territories where it was not necessary to spread Christianity by fire and sword, because the majority of the local population had been Christian for centuries and had known the feudal hierarchical system since Carolingian times; on these existing foundations it was possible to build a new state. It was only necessary to install one's own reliable people in suitable positions. It could easily happen that many of the former owners also found their place in the new order.

The significance of the raiding expeditions, as well as of the Battle of Bratislava in 907, lies in the fact that they provided enough time of grace during which it was possible by the end of the 10th century to create a consolidated state out of Pannonia, and the subjugation of the eastern part of the Carpathian Basin could also come in turn. In the eastern territories, where the foundations of Christianity and feudalism were lacking, the main burden of the work of extending the empire fell to the 11th-century descendants of the founding Árpáds: the princes Béla, Géza and Ladislaus. Those named – having been pushed out of the kingdom – were forced to persevere in these barbarian and pagan territories, to build up their power there and thus to extend the borders of the Hungarian state, unlike their royal relatives, who in the consolidated western part of the state were enjoying the fruits of their ancestors, the founders of the state. Only in the middle of the 11th century, after the dynastic conflicts within the Árpád family, did the Christian feudal state expand into the eastern parts of the Carpathian Basin as well.

It is clear to see that the most important ability is not conquest but adaptation, and that both for the population originally living here and for the conquerors and their leadership. As Darwinism also has it: life is preserved not by the strongest, the fastest or the cleverest, but by the one who can best adapt to changing conditions. This ability to adapt existed in the medieval Hungarian state too. It received and supported guests – immigrants – and accordingly retuned the machinery of state (sometimes more, sometimes less successfully), and it managed to maintain the integrity of the state continuously. The development of civic consciousness at the level of the Western countries was indeed delayed, and the lack of changes in infrastructure also led to a falling behind the countries of Western Europe, but it was only the Turkish invasion and the subsequent partition of the country that proved a fateful blow with irreversible consequences.

Our tragic Moon has become for us the erroneous interpretation of the conquest of the homeland, which has fossilised into a dogma. The truth is that Asimov would not have been a true intellectual had he not also written an essay answering himself, entitled „The Triumph of the Moon“, in which he argued that life on land too owes its existence to this heavenly body circling the Earth, more precisely to the tides it causes. We, however, cannot be quite such optimists: in our false view of history there is not a trace of triumph.
Translation: Kveta M.
